bib.title: LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models

read.skipped: Reference list skimmed only (lineage). Figure content (heat maps) not readable as text; captions read.

question: Can a large pre-trained language model be adapted to downstream tasks by training only low-rank updates to its weights, matching full fine-tuning quality with far fewer trainable parameters, less memory and no extra inference latency?
hypothesis: The change in weights during model adaptation has a low 'intrinsic rank', so a rank decomposition BA of the update suffices.
contributions: A shared pre-trained model can be used to build many small LoRA modules; tasks are switched by swapping A and B.
LoRA makes training more efficient and lowers the hardware barrier by up to 3 times with adaptive optimizers, since gradients and optimizer states are not kept for frozen parameters.
The linear design lets the trainable matrices be merged with frozen weights at deployment, with no inference latency versus a fully fine-tuned model.
LoRA is orthogonal to prior methods such as prefix-tuning (combination in Appendix E).
An empirical study of rank-deficiency in the adaptation update (Section 7).

method.summary: Freeze the pre-trained weights W0 and learn the update as a product BA of rank r, with B (d x r) initialised to zero and A (r x k) to a random Gaussian, so h = W0x + (alpha/r)BAx. In experiments it is applied only to attention projection matrices (mostly Wq and Wv), MLPs frozen. After training BA is added into W0 so inference cost is unchanged. Evaluated against full fine-tuning, BitFit, prefix-embedding/layer tuning and adapters on RoBERTa, DeBERTa XXL, GPT-2 M/L and GPT-3 175B.
method.task: parameter-efficient adaptation of pre-trained Transformer language models (NLU on GLUE, data-to-text NLG, NL-to-SQL, summarization)

datasets.name: GLUE (MNLI, SST-2, MRPC, CoLA, QNLI, QQP, RTE, STS-B)

datasets.source: Wang et al. 2019; individual datasets under different permissive licences
datasets.preprocessing: RoBERTa comparison with adapters: sequence length 128, same batch size for all tasks; MRPC, RTE, STS-B initialised from pre-trained model (not MNLI-adapted) for runs marked with a dagger

datasets.name: WebNLG
datasets.size: 22K examples in total, 14 categories (9 seen in training, 5 unseen)

datasets.name: WikiSQL
datasets.preprocessing: x = {table schema, query}, y = {SQL}; GPT-3 sequence length 384

datasets.name: MultiNLI (MNLI-m)
datasets.size: 392K train (MNLI-392K); low-data subsets of 100, 1k, 10k randomly sampled

datasets.name: SAMSum
datasets.preprocessing: context = utterances joined by newline then double newline; target = summary; GPT-3 sequence length 2048

other.note: layers inferred from '96 layers' in Section 7.1

models.name: LoRA
models.params: GPT-3: 4.7M (r_q=r_v=1 or r_v=2) and 37.7M (r_q=r_v=8 or r_q=r_k=r_v=r_o=2); RoBERTa base 0.3M; RoBERTa large 0.8M; DeBERTa XXL 4.7M; GPT-2 M 0.35M; GPT-2 L 0.77M
models.architecture: trainable A (r x k, Gaussian init) and B (d x r, zero init) added in parallel to frozen W; delta scaled by alpha/r
models.init_from: pre-trained base frozen; for GLUE MRPC/RTE/STS-B LoRA modules initialised from the best MNLI checkpoint except in dagger runs

other.trainable_params_formula: |Theta| = 2 x L_LoRA x d_model x r
other.alpha_rule: alpha set to the first r tried and not tuned
other.applied_to: Wq and Wv in most experiments; MLP, LayerNorm and biases not adapted

training.objective: conditional language modeling: max sum over (x,y) of sum_t log P(y_t | x, y_<t) (Eq. 1-2); classification tasks per GLUE metric
training.lr: GPT-3: 2.00E-04 for LoRA (5.00E-06 FT, 5.00E-04 PreEmbed, 1.00E-04 PreLayer, 1.6E-03 BitFit, 1.00E-04 AdapterH); GPT-2: 0.0002; RoBERTa base: 4E-04 to 5E-04; RoBERTa large: 2E-04 to 4E-04; DeBERTa XXL: 6E-05 to 2E-04 (per task, Tables 9-12)
training.warmup: RoBERTa: ratio 0.06; DeBERTa: ratio 0.1; GPT-2: 500 steps; GPT-3: 250,000 tokens
training.batch_size: GPT-3: 128 (MNLI-n: 20 for 100 and 1k, 100 for 10k, 128 for full); GPT-2: 8; RoBERTa base 16-32; RoBERTa large 4-8; DeBERTa XXL 4-32
training.epochs: GPT-3: 2 (MNLI-100 and 1k: 40, MNLI-10k: 4); GPT-2: 5; RoBERTa base 25-80; RoBERTa large 10-30; DeBERTa XXL 5-30
training.seq_len: GPT-3: 384 WikiSQL, 768 MNLI, 2048 SAMSum; RoBERTa fair-comparison runs: 128; RoBERTa base max 512; DeBERTa XXL max 64-512 by task
training.weight_decay: GPT-3: 0.1; GPT-2: 0.01 (E2E, WebNLG), 0.0 (DART); DeBERTa XXL: 0 to 0.1 by task
training.dropout: GPT-2: 0.1 (E2E, WebNLG), 0.0 (DART); DeBERTa CLS dropout 0 to 0.2
training.hardware: NVIDIA Tesla V100 for all experiments (latency study on NVIDIA Quadro RTX8000)
training.seeds: RoBERTa and DeBERTa: median over 5 random seeds, best epoch per run; GPT-2: mean over 3 random seeds, best epoch per run; GPT-3: only a typical standard deviation per task reported, not per entry

other.lora_config: RoBERTa and DeBERTa: r_q = r_v = 8; LoRA alpha 8 (RoBERTa base, DeBERTa), 16 (RoBERTa large); GPT-2: r_q = r_v = 4, alpha 32; GPT-3: LoRA hyperparameters r per Table 15
other.gpt3_throughput: 32.5 tokens/s per V100 for full fine-tuning vs 43.1 tokens/s per V100 for LoRA, same number of model-parallel shards (footnote 5)
other.tuning: learning rate tuned for every method-dataset combination on GPT-3; same hyperparameters across datasets after tuning lr
other.prefix_settings_gpt3: PreEmbed l_p=256, l_i=8 (3.2M); PreLayer l_p=8, l_i=8 (20.2M)
other.gpt2_baseline_hparams: batch size, lr and beam size follow Li & Liang 2021

inference.decoding: GPT-2 data-to-text: beam search, beam size 10, length penalty 0.9 (E2E) / 0.8 (WebNLG, DART), no repeat ngram size 4
inference.prompting: no prompting; fine-tuned with context-target pairs (e.g. x = table schema + query, y = SQL). Few-shot GPT-3 baseline in Appendix A: two demonstrations per class, six in-context examples in total for MNLI-matched

other.latency_study: single forward pass of GPT-2 medium, averaged over 100 trials on NVIDIA Quadro RTX8000, batch size 1 to 32, sequence length 128 to 512

metrics.name: GLUE accuracy / correlation
metrics.definition: overall matched+mismatched accuracy for MNLI, Matthew's correlation for CoLA, Pearson correlation for STS-B, accuracy for others

results.quote: LoRA can reduce the number of trainable parameters by 10,000 times and the GPU memory requirement by 3 times.
results.note: The 3x memory claim corresponds to the Section 4.2 numbers of 1.2TB to 350GB VRAM (about 3.4x). Intro says 'by up to 3 times'.

limits: Not straightforward to batch inputs for different tasks with different A and B in a single forward pass if A and B are merged into W; unmerged dynamic selection is possible where latency is not critical (Section 4.2).
Only attention weights adapted; MLP, LayerNorm and biases left to future work; the choice of which matrices to adapt is heuristic (Section 4.2, Section 8).
Authors do not expect a small r to work for every task: a task in a different language than pre-training could need r near d_model (footnote 6).
GPT-3 results are single runs with a typical-variance estimate rather than per-entry error bars, due to training cost; WikiSQL fluctuation +/-0.5% is as large as the gap to full fine-tuning.
Many baseline numbers are copied from prior work with differing setups; some baselines appear only in some experiments.
Rank study hyperparameters were tuned at r=4 for GPT-2, so other ranks may be sub-optimal (Table 18 caption).
Relationship between model size and optimal rank is left open; mechanism of why LoRA works is not established (Section 8).
Training memory saving requires the full frozen base model in VRAM; the 350GB model is still needed at deployment (footnote 4).
Dated: GPT-3, RoBERTa, DeBERTa-era evaluation; no instruction-tuned or chat models, no quantised base.

terms.definition: Low-Rank Adaptation: freezes the pre-trained weights and injects trainable rank decomposition matrices into each layer of the Transformer
the hypothesis that the update to weights during adaptation has low rank, so W0 + delta W = W0 + BA with r much smaller than min(d,k)
delta W x is scaled by alpha/r, alpha a constant in r; tuning alpha is roughly the same as tuning the learning rate and reduces retuning when r varies
ratio ||dW||_F / ||U^T W V^T||_F, how much dW amplifies the projection of W onto its subspace

code.snippet: W0 + ΔW = W0 + BA, where B ∈ R^{d×r}, A ∈ R^{r×k}, and the rank r ≪ min(d, k); delta Wx scaled by alpha/r; A random Gaussian, B zero
